title: Spatial Omics Rewrites the Computational Map of Drug Exposure, Target Engagement, Response, and Resistance.
Geometric Consequences of Bounded Phase Space Mechanics on Pharmacodynamics: Drug-Target Interaction, Dose-Response, and Selectivity
items.abstract: <jats:p>We derive pharmacodynamics from a single axiom: physical systems occupy bounded regions of phase space admitting partition and nesting. From this axiom we derive, inline, the partition coordinate system (n, ℓ, m, s) with capacity C(n) = 2n 2 , the partition depth M, the Composition Theorem, the Compression Theorem, and the Conservation Theorem. Drug Ptarget interaction follows as partition completion with binding energy E bind = T P k B ln b • ∆M and equilibrium dissociation K d = exp(-∆M bind ln b). Dose response follows from the universal equation of state P V = N k B T • S applied to target occupancy, producing five regime-specific curve shapes of which the Hill equation is the aperture limit. Selectivity is zero-work categorical filtering: Landauer's bound k B T ln 2 does not apply because target recognition is injective, not erasure. Allosteric regulation emerges as partition coupling through the protein's internal partition network, with propagation velocity v s ∼ κ/m eff ∼ 10 3 m/s. Receptor reserve and partial agonism are derived as corollaries. Drug-drug competition follows from Partition Conservation. Every quantity is derived inline from the axiom; no results are imported. The paper makes ten explicit, falsifiable predictions distinguishing it from conventional PD.</jats:p>

title: CortexLume: Rapid Geometry-Adaptive Cortical Feedback for Target-Informed fNIRS Design
items.abstract: Target-informed functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) probe design requires repeated evaluation of how candidate source-detector geometries sample the cortex, but full photon-transport modeling is too costly for interactive revision. We developed CortexLume, which couples an editable target-patch-placement representation with a geometry-adaptive cortical surrogate for rapid spatial assessment. The surrogate adapts its center, orientation, and anisotropic extent to fitted source-detector geometry and local scalp-cortex relationships, and is intended to approximate normalized cortical spatial allocation rather than absolute optical sensitivity. We benchmarked the method against MCX photon transport assembled through AtlasViewer on the ICBM152 anatomical model and then evaluated the frozen formulation on the independent Colin27 model without retuning. On ICBM152, mean channel-centroid discrepancy was 2.35 mm, 90%-mass Dice was 0.746 per channel and 0.826 per patch, and Jensen-Shannon distance was 0.330; the complete formulation improved Dice in 370 of 396 channels relative to a restricted reference. On Colin27, mean channel Dice was 0.748 and patch Dice was 0.812 across 88 retained channels. Patch-field construction required a median of only 75.81 ms. These results support CortexLume as a rapid cortical surrogate for iterative probe drafting and candidate shortlisting, with subject-specific photon modeling retained for final optical refinement.

title: Cell Wall Bioactive Molecules as Signaling and Effector Agents in Bacterial Adaptive Biology and Host Interactions
items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    The molecules that make up the bacterial cell wall should be viewed not only as passive structural components of the murein sacculus, which protect and enclose the inner membrane containing the bacterial cytoplasm. They are also bioactive molecules released during bacterial replication, especially after cell lysis, involving the disintegration of the cell wall. These molecules range in structure from simple acetylated monosaccharides or amino acids, such as
                    <jats:sc>d</jats:sc>
                    -amino acids, to more complex muropeptides and cross-linked peptides. They can be classified as cell wall bioactive molecules (CWBAMs), which have signaling and effector roles that influence bacterial physiology, including biofilm formation, sporulation, and antibiotic resistance. CWBAMs also participate in interactions with other bacteria, the microbiota, and immune cells from human and animal organs, including the central nervous system. The effects of CWBAMs released during cell wall breakdown remain largely unknown, especially since they can translocate from mucosal surfaces colonized by microbiota into the bloodstream. CWBAMs are not necessarily toxins and should be distinguished from endotoxins. Their role in bacterial–host interactions is a promising area for future research.
                  </jats:p>

title: Adaptive Vision-Based Feedback Systems: Enhancing Personalized Learning through Real-Time Emotion and Engagement Recognition
items.abstract: <jats:p>The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in educational environments has opened new opportunities to improve personalized learning experiences. This research explores the development of an adaptive vision-based feedback system that leverages computer vision and machine learning to monitor and analyze students' emotional states and engagement in real time. By recognizing non-verbal cues such as facial expressions, gaze direction, and posture, the system dynamically provides tailored pedagogical feedback. Our approach employs a hybrid architecture that combines convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with Vision Transformers (ViTs) to achieve robust emotion and engagement classification. Experiments on AffectNet and DAiSEE datasets, complemented by controlled classroom studies, show significant improvements in recognition accuracy and measurable benefits for learners' academic performance. Findings demonstrate that AI-driven affective computing can bridge the gap between cognition and emotion, enabling personalized, responsive, and inclusive education.</jats:p>
